11. Mr. Faruque Ahmed, the learned Advocate, thereafter argued that in the instant case, some of the material witnesses have not been produced in court without any explanation by the prosecution. He has pointed out that the Investigating Officer of this case Md. Awlad Hossain Khan who was shown as a charge-sheet witness, the Assistant Chemical Examiner, CID, Dhaka one Abdul Awal who chemically examined the seized incriminating powder and gave his report opining that the same contained heroin have not been examined in this case. Then again some other charge-sheet witnesses No. 5, Sub-Inspector, Abul Hashem and charge-sheet witness No. 6 Sub-Inspector Faruq Bepari who allegedly recorded and filled up the FIR form have also not been produced in court in this case. The learned advocate for the appellant further pointed out that the incriminating articles i.e. the powder allegedly containing heroin as well as the other articles allegedly seized and recovered from the house of the accused appellant, have also not been marked as any material exhibit in this case and, as such, according to him, by non-production of the aforesaid material witnesses, particularly the Investigating Officer and the chemical examiner and also non-production of the alamats of the case before the trial Court, an adverse presumption ought to have been drawn against the prosecution case as the defence was seriously prejudiced for their non-production in court. In support of his contention the learned Advocate for the appellant has relied on some decisions—one in the case of Nazir Ahmed & ors. Vs. State reported in 1985 BCR 279 and another in the case of Ismail Munshi Vs. State, 33 DLR 5 and another in the case of ARM Reza and others Vs. State reported in 9 DLR 594 and about non-production of alamats, he has relied on a decision in the case of Bangladesh Vs. Paran Chandra Baroi reported in 1986 BCR (AD) 225. 

 12. Mr. Enamul Hoque, the learned Advocate for the State, on the other hand, submitted the in view of section 134 of the Evidence Act, it was the quality and not the quantity of witnesses which was to be looked into and even conviction could be maintained on the basis of a single reliable and truthful solitary witness. As regards non-examination of the Investigating Officer, his submission was that unless it was shown that for such non-production of the Investigating Officer the defence was prejudiced, there should not be any adverse presumption drawn against the prosecution case and in this connection he relied on a decision in the case of Bhagaban Chandra Chakma Vs. State reported in 1987 BLD 351 = 38 DLR 374 and as regards non-production of some other witnesses, he submitted that if it was found that apart from those witnesses, the prosecution was able to prove its case beyond all reasonable doubt by the witness already produced then, non-production of any other witness or witnesses would not affect the merit of the prosecution case. In this connection, he relied on a decision in the case of Md. Abdul Karim Mondal Vs. Fazlul Bari and others reported in 33 DLR 397.  13. Now let me consider the above submissions of the learned Advocates on the points as raised; Admittedly the Investigating Officer Abdul Awal Khan and the chemical examiner were cited as witnesses in the charge-sheet, but none of them was produced as a witness. From a scrutiny of the records, it could not be found that the alamats including the incriminating articles along with the alleged heroin were produced before the trial Court and/or marked as material Exhibits. The alleged report of the chemical examiner was also not available in the record. The learned Advocate for the State only from the charge-sheet tried to show that the alamats were sent to the court at the time of submission of the charge-sheet and that the court presumably was the court of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, but thereafter nothing was available in the record to show any production of the alleged alamats to the court of trial. From the impugned judgment also it does not appear that the learned Additional Sessions Judge had any chance to see the alleged report of the chemical examiner or the other alamats in the case. So, it is doubtful whether these were at all produced before the trial Court and this situation could be explained, had the Investigating Officer and the chemical examiner been examined in this case and hence non- examination of these material witnesses undoubtedly caused serious prejudice to the accused. Thus, relying on the decisions cited by the learned Advocate for the appellant, it must be held that the learned Additional Sessions Judge committed illegality in not drawing an adverse presumption against the prosecution under section 114(g) of the Evidence Act. Of course, the report of the chemical examiner as per provision of sub-section 3 of section 50 of the said Act can be taken as a piece of evidence. But it is to be seen whether such chemical examination of the article was genuinely made by the chemical examiner and whether his report was actually available in the record. In the instant case no report is available.
